name: Head-to-Toe Assessment Checklist
description: A head-to-toe physical assessment checklist for nursing students and new nurses, in the order you would perform it at the bedside.

items.text: Perform hand hygiene, introduce yourself and confirm the patient's identity with two identifiers
Note general appearance, distress, hygiene, posture and behavior
Measure temperature, pulse, respirations, blood pressure and oxygen saturation
items.note: Count respirations without telling the patient, for example while you still appear to be taking the pulse. People breathe differently when they know they are being watched.

items.text: Rate pain with a scale the patient understands, and note location, quality and onset
Compare vital signs with the last set and the patient's baseline
Assess level of consciousness: alert, lethargic, obtunded or unresponsive
Check orientation to person, place, time and situation
Check pupils for PERRLA: equal, round, reactive to light and accommodation
Check hand grip and foot push strength on both sides
items.note: Weakness on one side that is new can be a sign of stroke. Report it right away and follow your facility's stroke protocol.

items.text: Note speech clarity and the ability to follow commands
Inspect the head and face for symmetry, lesions or injury
Inspect the eyes, ears and nose for drainage
Inspect the mouth for moist mucous membranes, teeth or dentures and lesions
Check that the trachea is midline and look for jugular vein distention
Inspect breathing pattern, effort, use of accessory muscles and chest shape
Auscultate lung sounds front and back, comparing side to side
items.note: Listen on bare skin, not through a gown. Have the patient breathe slowly through the mouth, and listen to a full breath in each spot.

items.text: Note adventitious sounds, such as crackles, wheezes, rhonchi or stridor
Note cough, sputum color and any oxygen device and flow rate
Auscultate heart sounds at the aortic, pulmonic, Erb's point, tricuspid and mitral areas
Count the apical pulse for a full minute if the rhythm is irregular
Palpate radial and pedal pulses on both sides and compare strength
Check capillary refill and skin color and temperature of hands and feet
Check for edema in the feet, ankles and legs and grade it per policy
Inspect the abdomen for shape, distention, scars and wounds
Auscultate bowel sounds in all four quadrants before palpating
items.note: Before you chart bowel sounds as absent, follow your facility's rule for how long to listen in each quadrant, which is often several minutes.

items.text: Lightly palpate for tenderness, firmness or masses, ending with any painful area
Ask about last bowel movement, nausea, appetite and diet tolerance
Note urine color, amount and any pain or trouble urinating
If a urinary catheter is in place, check that it is secured and the bag hangs below the bladder
Assess range of motion, muscle strength and gait if safe to walk
Inspect skin color, temperature, moisture, turgor and intact areas
Check pressure points such as the sacrum, heels and elbows for redness or breakdown
items.note: Press on any red area. If it doesn't blanch, it may be an early pressure injury.

items.text: Score pressure injury risk with the Braden Scale
items.note: Braden scores range from 6 to 23. A lower score means higher risk, and 18 or below is a common cutoff for starting prevention steps.

items.text: Complete a fall risk assessment with your facility's tool
Inspect IV sites for redness, swelling, pain, leaking and the dressing date
Check drains, tubes and wound dressings
Make sure the bed is low and locked and the call light is within reach
Document findings promptly and report abnormal or changed findings to the nurse or provider

faq.q: What order do you do a head-to-toe assessment in?
faq.a: Start with the general survey and vital signs, then neuro, HEENT and neck, respiratory, cardiovascular, abdomen, genitourinary, musculoskeletal and skin. Finish with pain, safety checks and documentation. Many schools teach a slightly different order, so follow the one your program grades.

faq.q: Why is the abdomen assessed in a different order?
faq.a: For the abdomen, nurses inspect, auscultate, percuss and then palpate. Pressing on the abdomen before listening can change bowel sounds, so you listen first.
The patient knows who they are, where they are, the date or time, and why they are there (the situation). If a patient knows only their name and location, you would chart them as oriented x2.

faq.q: How long should a head-to-toe assessment take?
faq.a: With practice, a routine head-to-toe assessment on a stable adult often takes around 10 to 20 minutes. Students are usually slower at first. Speed comes from doing the steps in the same order every time.
